mcqs.question: In the multi-level AMAT formula, what does a cache level's 'miss penalty' actually equal?
options: The AMAT of the next level down in the hierarchy
A fixed constant, typically 100 cycles regardless of the system
The hit time of the level above it
The total capacity of the next level down, in bytes
mcqs.explanation: The recursive insight is that a miss at level N has to go fetch from level N+1, so the cost of that miss is exactly whatever level N+1's own AMAT is — which itself may include further misses going deeper. It's not a fixed constant, has nothing to do with the level above's hit time, and capacity in bytes isn't a time quantity at all.

mcqs.question: Why does L2's local miss rate look much worse than its global miss rate?
options: Local and global miss rate are always numerically identical for L2
Local miss rate is measured only against accesses that already missed L1 — a harder subset — while global miss rate is measured against all original CPU accesses
Global miss rate only counts writes, while local miss rate counts both reads and writes
Local miss rate is a made-up metric with no formal definition
mcqs.explanation: Local miss rate's denominator is only the accesses that reached L2 at all (i.e., L1 misses) — a pre-filtered, harder-to-hit subset — while global miss rate's denominator is every access from the top of the hierarchy, making the same number of L2 misses look far smaller as a fraction of all accesses. The two are legitimately and predictably different, not identical, and the distinction has nothing to do with read/write splits.

mcqs.question: Doubling L1's associativity reduces its miss rate but adds 1 extra cycle to its hit time. Under what condition does this change make overall AMAT worse, not better?
options: It can never make AMAT worse if the miss rate improves at all
Only if the cache is fully associative already
If the added hit-time cost (paid on every access) outweighs the miss-penalty cycles saved by the lower miss rate
Only if L2 doesn't exist in the hierarchy
mcqs.explanation: AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty; the extra hit-time cycle is paid on literally every access (hit or miss), while the miss-rate improvement only pays off on the fraction of accesses that would have missed. If that trade is unfavorable, AMAT rises even though hit rate improved — which is exactly why you must compute both terms rather than assume higher hit rate wins.

mcqs.question: In the worked example, miss rate dropped by only 2 absolute percentage points (4% to 2%) but overall speedup was 1.72x. Why is the speedup disproportionately large?
options: Because CPI_ideal itself decreased when the cache changed
Because memory accesses per instruction also dropped alongside the miss rate
Because the miss penalty was recalculated to be smaller after the cache change
Because memory stalls dominated total CPI at the higher miss rate, so even a modest relative reduction in stall cycles removes a large share of total CPI
mcqs.explanation: At 4% miss rate, stall cycles (5.2) made up about 84% of total CPI (6.2) — so halving the stall term removes a large fraction of total cycles even though the miss rate only moved by 2 absolute points. CPI_ideal, accesses per instruction, and miss penalty were all held fixed in the example; only miss rate changed.

mcqs.question: Why can real measured stall time undershoot the value predicted by a naive `MissRate x MissPenalty` calculation on an out-of-order core?
options: Non-blocking caches let multiple independent misses overlap in flight via MSHRs, so their latencies partially overlap instead of summing
Miss penalty numbers in datasheets are always overestimated
Out-of-order cores never actually stall on cache misses
AMAT-style formulas only apply to in-order cores and are otherwise invalid
mcqs.explanation: MSHRs let the core track several outstanding misses at once; when the misses are independent, the pipeline overlaps their latency rather than serializing it, so real stalls land below the naive per-miss sum. The other options are false generalizations — datasheet penalties aren't systematically wrong, out-of-order cores do stall when the reorder buffer fills, and AMAT reasoning still applies, just needs an MLP correction.
